facts.fact_text: The Equality Institute held street demonstrations denouncing various serious human-rights abuses allegedly committed by the Ministry of the Interior and in Georgian prisons.
At around 2.20 p.m. on 29 June 2006, the applicants began a demonstration outside the Tbilisi Court of Appeal.
The purpose of the applicants' demonstration on 29 June 2006 was to express their support for Mr Shalva Ramishvili and Mr Davit Kokhreidze.
According to the applicants' written statements of 4 and 5 July 2006, the first applicant used a megaphone to utter slogans.
The first applicant uttered the slogan: "We should not have political prisoners in Georgia!"
The first applicant uttered the slogan: "We urge you to obey justice and not the private interests of a number of high officials!"
The first applicant uttered the slogan: "Give me justice or give me death!"
The first applicant's speech had lasted some three minutes when several uniformed court bailiffs approached the applicants.
According to the applicants, the court bailiffs restrained the applicants by force allegedly without prior warning or explanation.
The applicants were taken into the court-house after being restrained by the bailiffs.
The applicants were locked in the bailiffs' duty room of the court-house.
The case file contained five separate records of arrest, one for each applicant.
The arrest records stated that the applicants had been arrested on the basis of section 76(3) § 1 (f) of the Courts of Common Jurisdiction Act of 13 June 1997.

When the applicants were transferred to the Interior Ministry remand centre, they learnt that they had been detained on the basis of a decision of 29 June 2006 issued by the President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal.
The arrest records stated that the applicants had been arrested on the basis of section 76(3) § 1 (f) of the Courts of Common Jurisdiction Act of 13 June 1997.

The arrest records stated that the offenders had "breached public order" in the form of "contempt of court, insults, disregard of the bailiffs' lawful orders to stop the wrongdoing, resistance to the bailiffs, attempts to influence the court by actions and verbal expressions, impeding the administration of justice, and so on".
Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on the basis of which the applicants were sanctioned by the decision of 29 June 2006, was titled "Liability for breach of public order in court".

Article 208 § 6(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure provided that in the event of a breach of public order or contempt committed inside the court building, the President of the court shall be entitled to apply the measures envisaged by Article 208 against the offender.

Article 208 § 7 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provided that decisions of the presiding judge and of the President of the court under Article 208 shall be delivered by on-the-spot deliberations and without an oral hearing, and no appeal shall lie against them.
Subsequent to the Constitutional Court judgments of 15 December 2006, Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was significantly revised on 29 December 2006.

The newly added paragraph 8 of Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure explicitly gave court bailiffs the power to arrest a person who had either "breached public order in the court, was in contempt, or had obstructed the normal functioning of the court".

Under the revised Article 208 § 8 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, bailiffs were obliged to draw up a record of such arrests and to bring the offenders before the President of the relevant court within twenty-four hours.

Paragraphs 10 and 11 of the amended Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure stated that proceedings concerning the imposition of detention on an offender should always be adversarial and conducted at an oral hearing at which the offender would be given an opportunity to defend him or herself.

Under the amended Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, should the President decide to detain the offender, the latter was entitled to lodge an appeal against that decision with the higher court within the next forty-eight hours.

The arrest records stated that the offenders had "breached public order" in the form of "contempt of court, insults, disregard of the bailiffs' lawful orders to stop the wrongdoing, resistance to the bailiffs, attempts to influence the court by actions and verbal expressions, impeding the administration of justice, and so on".
One of the bailiffs stated in his memo that the applicants' actions had amounted to an encroachment upon the court's independence and impartiality.
Another bailiff stated in his memo that the wrongdoers had been trying to influence the court.

The decision of 29 June 2006 noted the bailiffs' version of the incident, namely that the applicants, "who were inside the court building, in its central entrance, were breaching public order, obstructing the normal functioning of the court and seeking to influence the court with respect to proceedings in a particular case".
The decision of 29 June 2006 noted that despite the bailiffs' request that they stop the disturbance, the applicants persisted with their conduct in the form of "verbal expressions and actions".

The President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, Mrs E.T., concluded in the decision of 29 June 2006 that the applicants had "breached public order, shown manifest and gross contempt towards the court and endangered the administration of justice".
Article 208 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on the basis of which the applicants were sanctioned by the decision of 29 June 2006, was titled "Liability for breach of public order in court".
According to the applicants' written statements of 4 and 5 July 2006, the applicants stopped ten to twenty metres from the court-house.
According to the applicants, nothing was displayed or addressed to the court which could be construed as contempt during the incident of 29 June 2006.
According to the applicants, the absence of contempt during the incident of 29 June 2006 could be confirmed by independent eyewitnesses to the incident.
According to the applicants, the absence of contempt during the incident of 29 June 2006 could be confirmed by images filmed by a cameraman from the 202 television channel.

Judge Z.M. found in the decision of 26 July 2006 that it was established from the case materials that the applicants had truly exhibited "manifest and gross contempt" towards the Tbilisi Court of Appeal by committing those acts "inside the court building, namely in its central entrance hall".

Judge Z.M. stated in the decision of 26 July 2006 that the aim of Article 208 § 6(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was to protect public order not only inside court-houses but also outside them, in adjacent premises.

Judge Z.M. stated in the decision of 26 July 2006 that the President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal had no other choice but to sanction the applicants under Article 208 § 6(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, since what was at stake was "not the judge's own interests but the authority of the court and the proper administration of justice".

Section 76(4) § 1 of the Courts of Common Jurisdiction Act of 13 June 1997 specified that the right to resort to physical force, special equipment and firearms could be exercised only if other less severe measures of constraint had been shown to be ineffective.

The Constitutional Court stated in its judgment of 15 December 2006 that achieving and maintaining the protection of the authority of the courts and the smooth functioning of the justice system should not be carried out at the expense of the impairment of fundamental human rights.
The Equality Institute held public press conferences denouncing various serious human-rights abuses allegedly committed by the Ministry of the Interior and in Georgian prisons.

In reply to the complaint that the President of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal had made her decision entirely on the basis of one-sided submissions, Judge Z.M. stated in the decision of 26 July 2006 that all the evidence — the records of the applicants' arrest and the explanatory notes — had been drafted and submitted by the bailiffs for consideration by the President in accordance with a procedure envisaged by law.

Under Articles 252, 263 and 264 of the Code on Administrative Offences, a person charged with an administrative offence had the right to benefit from legal assistance during the examination of the case.
